title: Macquarie fined over 'welcome rates'
full_text:
Macquarie Bank will pay a fine and has compensated tens of thousands of customers after publishing a confusing description of how its "welcome" interest rate operates on deposits.
The penalties come amid intensifying regulatory scrutiny of savings account rates and fees as interest rates rise.
Macquarie, the fastest-growing player in retail banking with $116 billion in customer deposits and a 6.5 per cent share, stopped offering "welcome rates" in September.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission said Macquarie admitted to contravening the Corporations Act and agreed to a $14 million penalty in the NSW Supreme Court.
This came after the bank failed to take "necessary steps" to ensure statements about its welcome rate were clear, and operating systems and controls were not rigorous enough. Macquarie has pledged to improve its governance.
In addition to the fine, Macquarie has paid $8.8 million in remediation to almost 40,000 customers after identifying nine customer complaints linked to the issue after a case before the Australian Financial Complaints Authority.
ASIC said it would apply "enhanced supervision" to the banking sector to ensure customers received the interest rate promised by banks, amid confusion about bonus and base rate offers.
The offending Macquarie descriptions were made between December 2021 and September 2022, when it advertised its welcome rate as a "welcome variable rate" or "bonus offer".
When interest rates increased during 2022, the initial margin between the welcome rate and the standard variable rate could narrow or disappear. If the standard rate rose above the welcome rate, the customer's rate increased only to match the standard rate.
"This wasn't just unclear wording. Macquarie's systems and controls were not rigorous enough to identify the risk that customers would misunderstand how the welcome rate worked," said ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland on Tuesday. "At a time when Australians are contending with cost-of-living pressures, consumers deserve clear information about savings rates and the financial benefits they are promised."
Macquarie has stopped the welcome rates. "The welcome rate offer ended at 11.59pm (AEST) Monday, 14 September 2026," its website says.
Earlier this year, it was offering an extra 35 basis points over the ongoing variable rate when a savings account was opened online, on balances up to $250,000, for four months from account opening.
Macquarie's head of banking and financial services, Ben Perham, said the bank's customers "rightly have high expectations of us".
"Although ASIC has acknowledged our actions were not deliberate, we should have better explained on our website how the welcome rate would be applied, and we apologise for any confusion caused." said Perham.
"We have conducted a thorough review of all product descriptions we use across our website ... and have prioritised the uplift of our governance, systems, controls, and procedures associated with the creation, approval and publishing of any future customer-facing collateral."
Wednesday's action follows an ASIC investigation into mortgage offset accounts across the industry, which triggered a parliamentary inquiry.
The regulator said customers may unknowingly have paid more interest than they should. Banks paid more than $55 million in compensation.
Bonus rates have been under scrutiny for several years. The ACCC found 71 per cent of bonus interest accounts did not receive the bonus interest rate each month in the first half of 2023 during a review of deposit products.
Nine Entertainment Co.
